figures.caption: Figure 14.1 (top left panel) A simple stump, defined in Equation (14.1). (top right panel) A graphical illustration of a stump function as a binary tree. (bottom left panel) A depth two tree formed by recursing on each leaf of the stump, replacing it with a new stump. (bottom right panel) A graphical illustration of the depth two tree.

Figure 14.2 Four instances of (top row) a depth D = 2 tree unit and (bottom row) a depth D = 10 tree unit, where in each instance all the parameters (split points and leaf values) are set at random. The latter has higher capacity and is thus capable of generating a wider swath of shapes given diﬀerent settings of its parameters. Note here that the leaves are connected by vertical lines in order to give each tree instance a continuous appearance, which is done for visualization purposes only.

Figure 14.4 (top left panel) A prototypical nonlinear regression dataset. (top right panel) Three stumps with fixed leaf values (whose split point can vary). (middle panel) Each stump instance is slid horizontally across the input of the data by varying its split point value, creating three corresponding staircase-like Least Squares costs. (bottom panel) Each cost in the middle panel is constant in-between consecutive inputs, implying that we need only test one split point per flat region, e.g., the mid-point, as shown in this panel. See text for further details.
Figure 14.3 (left panel) Three stumps, each depicted in a distinct color. (right panel) A depth two tree (in black) created by adding together the three stumps shown in the left panel.

In this Section we discuss the application of tree-based universal approximators to the problem of classification, often referred to as classification trees.
we refer to the trees as having a maximum depth, i.e., the largest depth that a branch of the tree can possibly grow to.

we must test out an array of split point candidates to determine which works best. Once again, for the same practical purposes we saw with regression, we can simply test the mid-points between each consecutive pair of input values
the leaf values for a single stump-based model can be intuitively set to the mean output of those points belonging to each leaf of the stump
lean towards using the mode (i.e., the most popular output label), also called the majority vote.

To compensate for class imbalances like the one shown here we can, in complete analogy to the concept of weighting cost functions to better handle class imbalance (see Section 6.8.1), choose leaf values based on the balanced mode or balanced majority vote.
often these sorts of costs are approximately minimized by applying just a single step of Newton's method
in the context of classification trees quality metrics are often referred to as purity metrics, since they measure how pure each leaf of the stump is in terms of class representation.
with the balanced accuracy discussed in Section 6.8.4 being the safest choice given the class imbalance we might encounter in practice
With classification one natural halting condition is when a leaf is completely pure, that is, it contains only members of a single class.
trees are indeed the most popular universal approximator used when applying boosting-based cross-validation, with this pairing very often referred to as gradient boosting.
In the context of tree-based units this leads to the use of shallow trees, with stumps and trees of depth two being especially popular.

figures.caption: Figure 14.1 (top left panel) A simple stump, defined in Equation (14.1). (top right panel) A graphical illustration of a stump function as a binary tree. (bottom left panel) A depth two tree formed by recursing on each leaf of the stump, replacing it with a new stump. (bottom right panel) A graphical illustration of the depth two tree.

Figure 14.2 Four instances of (top row) a depth D = 2 tree unit and (bottom row) a depth D = 10 tree unit, where in each instance all the parameters (split points and leaf values) are set at random. The latter has higher capacity and is thus capable of generating a wider swath of shapes given diﬀerent settings of its parameters. Note here that the leaves are connected by vertical lines in order to give each tree instance a continuous appearance, which is done for visualization purposes only.

Figure 14.4 (top left panel) A prototypical nonlinear regression dataset. (top right panel) Three stumps with fixed leaf values (whose split point can vary). (middle panel) Each stump instance is slid horizontally across the input of the data by varying its split point value, creating three corresponding staircase-like Least Squares costs. (bottom panel) Each cost in the middle panel is constant in-between consecutive inputs, implying that we need only test one split point per flat region, e.g., the mid-point, as shown in this panel. See text for further details.
